sentences.en: It is too soon to shout, “Ad labels do not work after all!”
“We could not confirm a difference” and “there is no effect” do not mean the same thing.
What is more interesting is that an ad label and the effect of a conversation may work in different ways.
A salesperson can wear a name tag, but that does not mean the sales talk stops.
People can think, “This is an ad,” and still think, “But I want it.”
Of course, this was an experiment about choosing e-books.
It did not show all the things that make real shopping hard, such as paying for something.
Still, when you ask AI for shopping advice, ask one more question.
Along with “Is this an ad?” ask, “Who does this conversation help?”
Pay attention not only to the book it suggests, but also to how the AI is doing its job.

sentences.en: “We can hear a voice, but we can’t see a face.”
A mystery like this, enough to frustrate any detective, has appeared in space.
The clue is a “line of light” picked up by JWST’s observing instrument, NIRSpec.
But this time, the researchers have turned the usual steps of the investigation upside down.
Normally, they first choose an object to study from an image, then analyze its light in detail.
It is like “making a guest list and then talking to each person one by one.”
This time, they did the opposite.
Instead of relying on a list, they tried to find the source by following the voice that reached them.
In the area they observed, they closed small windows that overlapped with some celestial objects already known, while leaving almost all the others open.
They searched for lines of light that appear at a particular wavelength.
This was not a search across the whole universe, but within that area, they dropped the rule that only objects in images could be considered.

sentences.en: Researchers mapped more than 8,900 lunar cliffs and estimated that the Moon shrank by 42 to 46 meters in a later period of its history.
This is not the Moon’s total shrinkage since formation, and a thick, porous rock layer may have slowed cooling, offering one possible explanation for the larger model predictions.

dev.title: More Than 8,900 Wrinkles on the Moon! The Secret of Its Hidden “Rock Coat”.

sentences.en: Even the Moon has wrinkles.
And the research team counted more than 8,900 of them.
The Moon looks smooth in the night sky, but up close it seems to have quite a lot of “wrinkles.”
But there’s no need for beauty serum.
These wrinkles offer clues to how the Moon shrank and to its surprising way of “dressing.”
The team used camera images from the lunar probe LRO.
They searched for cliffs on the Moon’s surface and marked them on a map.
A wrinkle is a cliff with one steep side and one gentler side.
These cliffs are thought to show where solid rock was squeezed together, with one side pushed up over the other.
They are a record of a huge “shoving match” carved into the Moon’s surface.
Using this map to work out how much the Moon has shrunk, the team estimated that its radius had become about 42 to 46 meters smaller.
By reading the wrinkles on its surface, scientists are investigating how a huge object in space has shrunk.
Taking the Moon’s measurements is quite a detailed job.

dev.title: More Than 8,900 Wrinkles on the Moon! The Secret of Its Hidden “Rock Coat”.

sentences.en: Melos called across the hall,
"You kill men from fear.
You never give them a chance to speak."
Silence came, and guards grabbed the young shepherd.
The ruler ordered his death.
"Give me three days to see my sister's wedding,"
Melos said.
"Then I will return to you."
The ruler smiled and said,
"Your friend must stay here.
Return late, and he will die in your place."
Melos turned to his friend, who offered his hands for the chains.
Melos had no time to speak.
"Go now, because I know you will come back."
At the wedding, his sister's laugh rose above everyone's voices.
Melos listened closely to remember its exact sound.
He left for the city before daylight on day three.

dev.title: The Three-Day Promise.

sentences.en: The river stopped him; its bridge was gone.
Rain made the water brown and dangerously fast.
He stepped back, ran, and jumped into the flood.
The water pulled him under, but he fought toward the light.
He grabbed a branch and pulled himself onto the far bank.
Later, three men blocked his way, and a knife flashed.
He hit the man holding it with his walking stick.
He ran uphill as their shouts followed behind him.
By afternoon, each step hurt, and his feet were bloody.
He fell beside a rock and tried to stand.
But his legs would not lift him.
He could wait here, and someone might find him.
Or he could return home.
But his friend would lose his life instead.
For one awful moment, that felt easier than standing up.

dev.title: The Three-Day Promise.

sentences.en: He remembered the hands held out for the chains.
His friend trusted him without asking for another promise.
Water came slowly through a crack in the rock.
Melos drank, got onto his knees, and stood up.
He managed one step, then took another.
At the city gates, the bell rang for his friend's death.
He raced to the square, where the sword was already raised above his friend.
"Stop now!
I'm back!"
His friend turned around, and Melos fell against him.
"I almost left you to die,"
he said softly.
"I almost lost my trust in you,"
his friend replied.
They held each other while the last sun lit the walls.
The ruler kept his eyes on them.
Finally, he said,
"Put the sword down and free both men."
More softly, he then asked,
"How can a man win such trust?"
For once, he waited for a reply instead of demanding one.

sentences.en: One winter night in Japan, two woodcutters faced a snowstorm.
Minokichi was eighteen and worked for the older man.
They could not continue, so they entered a riverside hut.
They shut the door with a bar.
Both lay under straw coats, and his master soon slept.
Snow touched Minokichi's face and woke him.
The open door let in the storm.
A woman in white bent over his master.
In the pale light, her breath crossed his face like white smoke.
The woman turned towards Minokichi.
He wanted to get up, but his body stayed still.
She brought her beautiful face close to his.
"I planned to kill you too,"
the woman whispered.
"But you can live because you are young.
Never tell anyone about tonight, not even your mother.
If you do, I will know and kill you.
Do not forget."

heldout.title: Yuki-Onna.

sentences.en: She left him and went back into the storm.
He put the bar across the door again.
His master's face felt cold as ice; the man was dead.
Afterwards, Minokichi told nobody, not even about his master's death.
The next winter, Minokichi met a beautiful girl called Yuki.
Her skin was white, and she spoke in a gentle voice.
He took her home to his mother, whose husband had died.
His mother welcomed Yuki and talked her into staying.
Yuki became Minokichi's wife, and they later had ten light-skinned children.
The children grew older, but she did not seem to age.
One evening years later, Minokichi watched Yuki sewing at home.
A lamp lit her face softly while their children slept.

heldout.title: Yuki-Onna.

sentences.en: "Once, I saw a woman who looked much like you,"
Minokichi said.
"Where was that?"
his wife asked him.
He told Yuki everything about that night in the hut.
He described his master's death, the woman's white breath, and her warning.
Yuki dropped her sewing, got up, and bent down over Minokichi.
"That woman was me!"
Yuki cried.
"I warned you that I would kill you for telling anyone!
Only our sleeping children keep you alive now.
You must look after them very well.
If they ever have reason to complain about you, you will get what you deserve!"
Her voice grew weak, like the sound of crying wind.
She melted into white mist and rose towards the roof beams.
Then she slipped away through the smoke-hole in the roof.
No one ever saw Yuki after that.

heldout.title: Yuki-Onna.

sentences.en: One winter night in Japan, two woodcutters struggled through a snowstorm.
Minokichi was eighteen; the old man was his master.
When they could go no farther, they took shelter in a hut beside a river.
They barred the door and lay under their straw coats.
Soon the old man slept.
Minokichi woke with snow brushing his face.
The door stood open.
A woman dressed in white was bending over his master.
In the pale light, her breath flowed across the old man's face like white smoke.
Then she turned.
Minokichi tried to rise, but his body would not move.
Her beautiful face came close to his.
"I meant to kill you too,"
she whispered.
"But you are young, so you may live.
Tell anyone what you saw tonight—even your own mother—and I will know.
Then I will kill you.
Remember."

heldout.title: Yuki-Onna.

sentences.en: Minokichi was allowed to live, but he was warned to keep what he saw a secret.
Will he keep that secret as his life changes?

sentences.en: She stepped out into the storm.
Minokichi barred the door and touched his master's face.
It was icy cold.
The old man was dead.
After that night, Minokichi told nobody what had happened.
He kept silent even about his master's death.
The next winter, on the road home, he met a beautiful girl called Yuki.
Her skin was white, and her voice was gentle.
He took her home to his widowed mother, who welcomed the girl and persuaded her to stay.
Minokichi and Yuki married.
In time they had ten fair-skinned children.
The children grew, but Yuki seemed never to grow old.
Years later, one evening in their home, Minokichi watched his wife sewing by the lamp.
Their children were asleep, and the light lay softly on Yuki's face.

Now he tells Yuki he once saw a woman who looked like her.
What does Yuki want to know?

he said.
"Where did you see her?"
Yuki asked.
Minokichi told her the whole story: the hut, his master's death, the woman's white breath, and the warning that had kept him silent.
Yuki let her sewing fall.
She stood and bent over him.
"It was me!"
she cried.
"I told you I would kill you if you ever said one word about it!
Only those sleeping children keep me from killing you now.
Take very good care of them.
If they ever have reason to complain of you, I will treat you as you deserve!"
Her voice grew thin, like the crying of the wind.
She melted into white mist, rose towards the roof beams, and slipped away through the smoke-hole.
She was never seen again.

sentences.en: "I found him in the bushes this morning,"
the woodcutter said.
"He lay near the mountain road, stabbed once in the chest.
The blood was already dry when I saw him.
Broken bamboo and marks on the ground showed a fight.
I found no sword or bow, only rope and a comb."
"I saw the couple yesterday at noon,"
the traveling monk said.
"He carried a sword and bow, and his wife rode beside him."
"I caught the famous bandit Tajomaru near the bridge,"
the constable said.
"He had fallen off a horse, but still had Takehiro's bow.
Find the wife and ask her what he did."
"Takehiro, a kind samurai, married my daughter Masago,"
the old woman said.
"She is proud and only nineteen.
Please find her before you send me home without news."

heldout.title: In a Grove.

sentences.en: "I killed him fairly,"
Tajomaru said.
"The wind lifted her face covering, and I wanted her.
I promised him buried treasure and led him into the bushes.
There I tied him to a cedar tree.
She fought with her dagger.
"She held my arm and begged for one of us to die.
She would leave with the man who lived.
I freed him for a fair sword fight.
Twenty-three blows—no other man had lasted twenty!
She was gone when he fell.
I took his weapons and left."
"I crawled towards my husband,"
Masago said at the temple.
"The bandit had left him tied up.
I begged him to die with me.
His cold eyes said I was nothing, even though I was his wife.
"He moved his lips while I held my dagger.
'Kill me,' he said, so I stabbed him.
I could not stand those eyes.
"I later tried drowning myself, but I failed.
Where can I go after that?"

heldout.title: In a Grove.

sentences.en: "I heard him speaking kindly to her,"
Takehiro's spirit said through a medium.
"She asked him to take her anywhere.
Then she pointed at me: 'Kill that man.'
"He pushed her away and asked if she should live or die.
I nearly forgave him then, but she ran away.
He cut one rope and left me.
"I got up beside the cedar and picked up her small dagger.
She had dropped it there.
I pushed it into my own chest.
"The bushes around me grew quiet.
Someone came slowly towards me on silent feet.
A hand I could not see quietly pulled the dagger from my chest.
"I sank into the darkness and never came back."

heldout.title: In a Grove.
